etymology: From Latin perversus, turned about, from pervertere, to overturn. Webster 1828: obstinate in the wrong; stubborn; untractable; also, distorted from the right. In the Authorized Version it describes a way, a generation, a heart, a tongue, and a kind of religious argument — in every case something straight that has been turned.
biblical_def: Perverse is not merely bad; it is bent. The angel who withstands Balaam says exactly that: I went out to withstand thee, because thy way is perverse before me (Numbers 22:32). The word is a verdict on direction. Proverbs applies it to the organs of speech and the seat of the will: perverse lips put far from thee (Proverbs 4:24); he that is of a perverse heart shall be despised (Proverbs 12:8); he that hath a perverse tongue falleth into mischief (Proverbs 17:20). Job, examining himself honestly, admits that if he claims perfection his own mouth shall also prove me perverse (Job 9:20). The New Testament keeps the word for a whole society and for a whole party in the church. Our Lord calls His own generation faithless and perverse (Matthew 17:17); Paul tells the Philippians they shine as lights in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation (Philippians 2:15); and he warns the Ephesian elders that of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them (Acts 20:30). The last is the sharpest use. Perversity is not always coarse; it can be articulate, ecclesiastical, and internal, and Paul says it comes from inside the eldership.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PERVERSE as obstinate in the wrong; disposed to be contrary; stubborn; untractable; and, in a second sense, distorted from the right or true. Both are biblical: a bent way and a stubborn will.
webster_full: PERVERSE, a. [L. perversus.] — Literally, turned aside; hence, distorted from the right.
Obstinate in the wrong; disposed to be contrary; stubborn; untractable.
Cross; petulant; peevish; disposed to cross and vex.

Webster’s literal sense is the key: the word does not begin as a moral insult but as a description of direction. A perverse way is a way turned aside, and the moral force follows from the fact that there was a right road to turn from.
scriptures: Numbers 22:32
And the angel of the LORD said unto him, Wherefore hast thou smitten thine ass these three times? behold, I went out to withstand thee, because thy way is perverse before me:
Proverbs 12:8
A man shall be commended according to his wisdom: but he that is of a perverse heart shall be despised.
Proverbs 17:20
He that hath a froward heart findeth no good: and he that hath a perverse tongue falleth into mischief.
Philippians 2:15
That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world;
Acts 20:30
Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.
corruption_summary: The word is corrupted by relativism, which denies the straight line that perversity presupposes: if there is no right way, nothing can be turned aside from it, and Acts 20:30 becomes merely a description of diversity.
corruption_paragraphs: Every use of perverse in Scripture assumes a straight road. Balaam’s way was perverse before the LORD, measured against a standard external to Balaam. Where a culture has decided there is no such standard, the word survives only as an insult and loses its content entirely. This is not a marginal loss. Proverbs builds a whole moral education on the contrast between the straight and the crooked — the upright walk, the froward mouth, the perverse tongue — and none of it can be taught to a student who has been told in advance that the road is whatever each traveller makes of it.

Acts 20:30 names the specific danger and it is internal. Paul does not warn the Ephesian elders chiefly about pagan Ephesus; he warns them that men will arise of your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw disciples after them. The motive named is a following. That is how doctrinal corruption has actually entered churches in every century — through ordained men with a gift for speech who wanted a party. The safeguards Scripture gives are plurality of elders, a written confession, and a congregation that knows the Scriptures well enough to hear when the road has bent. Paul’s own remedy in the next verse is the word of God’s grace, which is able to build you up, and to give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified.
roots_summary: The Hebrew words are from roots meaning to twist, bend, or make crooked; the Greek diastrepho means to distort or turn aside thoroughly, and it is the word behind both our Lord’s perverse generation and Paul’s warning to the elders.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'iqqesh (H6141) — twisted, crooked, perverse; used of the heart, the lips, and the way (Proverbs 12:8; 17:20).
Hebrew yarat (H3399) — to be precipitate or headlong; behind thy way is perverse before me (Numbers 22:32).
Greek diastrepho (G1294) — to distort, turn aside thoroughly, pervert; a crooked and perverse nation (Philippians 2:15), speaking perverse things (Acts 20:30).
Greek paradiatribe — the perverse disputings of 1 Timothy 6:5, constant friction among men of corrupt minds.
The Latin pervertere, to overturn, gives the English its picture: not a wrong invented but a right overturned.
usage: Thy way is perverse before me (Numbers 22:32) — a direction judged against a standard outside the traveller.
A crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights (Philippians 2:15) — the diagnosis and the calling in one sentence.
Of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things (Acts 20:30) — the corruption Paul expects comes from inside the eldership.

etymology: From filth, Old English fylth, foulness. Webster 1828: dirty; foul; nasty; and, morally, obscene or polluted. The Authorized Version uses it for the whole race under sin, for the best works of unregenerate men, for a manner of speech, for a motive in ministry, and for the final fixing of character in Revelation.
biblical_def: Filthy in Scripture is a verdict, and the verses that carry it are among the most humbling in the Bible. Of the whole race the psalmist says, They are all gone aside, they are all together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one (Psalm 14:3) — a text Paul quotes in Romans 3 to close every mouth. Isaiah measures not our sins but our best: all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags (Isaiah 64:6). Zechariah shows the remedy in a vision: Now Joshua was clothed with filthy garments, and stood before the angel (Zechariah 3:3), and the garments are taken away and a change of raiment given. The New Testament turns the word to particulars. Speech: put off… filthy communication out of your mouth (Colossians 3:8). Money: an elder must not be greedy of filthy lucre (1 Timothy 3:3), and neither must a deacon (1 Timothy 3:8). Lot was vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked (2 Peter 2:7). And Revelation ends the matter with terrible finality: he which is filthy, let him be filthy still (Revelation 22:11). The word therefore spans the diagnosis, the cleansing, and the fixed state of those who refuse it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FILTHY as dirty; foul; nasty; and, morally, polluted, obscene, or gross. The KJV applies the word to the state of fallen man, to the works he calls righteous, to speech, and to a motive in ministry.
webster_full: FILTHY, a. — Dirty; foul; nasty; defiled with filth.
Morally, polluted; obscene; gross; as filthy language; filthy lucre.
Webster’s second sense preserves the KJV phrase filthy lucre, which does not mean that money is filth but that a greedy motive in a minister is; the qualifier is on the man’s desire, not on the coin.
scriptures: Psalm 14:3
They are all gone aside, they are all together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one.
Isaiah 64:6
But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags; and we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away.
Zechariah 3:3
Now Joshua was clothed with filthy garments, and stood before the angel.
1 Timothy 3:8
Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre;
Revelation 22:11
He that is unjust, let him be unjust still: and he which is filthy, let him be filthy still: and he that is righteous, let him be righteous still: and he that is holy, let him be holy still.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 64:6 is corrupted whenever filthy rags is softened into a comment about human imperfection, and Revelation 22:11 whenever the fixing of character at the end is replaced with the hope of endless second chances.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 64:6 does not say that our sins are filthy rags. It says our righteousnesses are. That is the doctrine of total depravity stated at its sharpest: the fall reaches not only the obviously wicked acts of unregenerate men but their virtues, their charity, and their religion, because the whole man — mind, will, and affections — is turned from God. Preaching that reduces this to a modest confession of imperfection has removed the reason a Substitute is needed. The counterpart is Zechariah 3, where the filthy garments are not laundered but removed, and a change of raiment is given: the imputed righteousness of Christ, which is the only clothing in which a sinner stands before the angel of the LORD.

Revelation 22:11 is the other end. He which is filthy, let him be filthy still is spoken near the close of the canon, and it announces the fixing of character — a point past which the unjust and the filthy are confirmed as they are. This forecloses universalism and post-mortem probation alike. The gospel offers no endless supply of later opportunities; it offers a present cleansing. Nor does the verse license fatalism now, for the same chapter says whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely. The urgency of the invitation is the reason the fixing is announced.
roots_summary: Several words stand behind the English: a Hebrew root for becoming tainted or sour, the Hebrew for menstrual cloth in Isaiah 64:6, and Greek terms for shameful speech and shameful gain.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'alach (H444) — to be turned, tainted, morally corrupt; all together become filthy (Psalm 14:3; 53:3).
Hebrew 'iddim in Isaiah 64:6 — the word for a menstrual cloth, the most ceremonially unclean rag in the household; the KJV renders it filthy rags.
Hebrew tsoi (H6674) — filthy, excremental; Joshua’s garments before the angel (Zechariah 3:3).
Greek aischrologia (G148) — shameful speaking; filthy communication out of your mouth (Colossians 3:8).
Greek aischrokerdes (G146) — greedy of shameful gain; the disqualification for elders and deacons (1 Timothy 3:3, 8).
usage: All our righteousnesses are as filthy rags (Isaiah 64:6) — our virtues, not merely our sins, come under the verdict.
Not greedy of filthy lucre (1 Timothy 3:8) — a qualification for office; the filth is in the motive, not the money.
He which is filthy, let him be filthy still (Revelation 22:11) — character fixed at the end; no second probation.

etymology: From fool, through Old French fol, from Latin follis, a bellows or windbag. Webster 1828: void of understanding or sound judgment; unwise; also, sinful. In Scripture the word is never merely intellectual. The foolish man is not the man with a low intelligence but the man who has set himself against the fear of the LORD.
biblical_def: Biblical folly is a moral condition. Moses charges the nation: Do ye thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise? is not he thy father that hath bought thee? (Deuteronomy 32:6). The fault is ingratitude to a Redeemer, not a deficiency of intellect. The psalms put the foolish under God’s hatred alongside the workers of iniquity: The foolish shall not stand in thy sight: thou hatest all workers of iniquity (Psalm 5:5). Asaph confesses his own bout of it: So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee (Psalm 73:22) — and what made him foolish was envying the prosperity of the wicked. Our Lord divides the ten virgins by it: five of them were wise, and five were foolish (Matthew 25:2), the difference being oil, that is, preparedness for a delayed return. Paul calls the Galatians foolish for a doctrinal reason: O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you, that ye should not obey the truth (Galatians 3:1) — they had begun in the Spirit and turned back to the law. And Paul turns the word inside out: God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise (1 Corinthians 1:27). The cross is folly to men and wisdom in fact, which means the world’s scale of foolishness is itself upside down.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FOOLISH as void of understanding or sound judgment; unwise; and adds the scriptural sense — sinful, wicked, acting without regard to the divine law. Both senses are required to read the Bible’s use.
webster_full: FOOLISH, a. — Void of understanding or sound judgment; weak in intellect; unwise; as, a foolish man.
Unwise; imprudent; acting without judgment or discretion in particular things.
In Scripture, wicked; sinful; acting without regard to the divine law and glory, or to one’s own eternal happiness.

Webster’s third sense is the one that unlocks the Psalms and Proverbs. The fool of Scripture is defined by his relation to God, and his want of judgment is the consequence of that relation, not the cause of it.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 32:6
Do ye thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise? is not he thy father that hath bought thee? hath he not made thee, and established thee?
Psalm 5:5
The foolish shall not stand in thy sight: thou hatest all workers of iniquity.
Psalm 73:22
So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee.
Matthew 25:2
And five of them were wise, and five were foolish.
Galatians 3:1
O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you, that ye should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you?
corruption_summary: The word is corrupted when folly is reduced to an intellectual deficiency — which makes the Bible’s warnings sound like snobbery — and when the modern refusal to make moral judgments removes the category altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: If foolish means unintelligent, then Psalm 5:5 makes God the hater of the slow-witted, and Deuteronomy 32:6 becomes an insult rather than an indictment. The Hebrew will not allow it. The fool of Scripture is a man who has said in his heart there is no God (Psalm 14:1), who despises instruction, who is right in his own eyes. Some of the most brilliant men of every century qualify, and some of the least educated do not. The distinction matters pastorally: folly in the biblical sense is repented of, not diagnosed, and its cure is the fear of the LORD, which Proverbs calls the beginning of knowledge.

1 Corinthians 1:27 is the corrective the age most needs and least expects. God has chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, which means the world’s ranking of what is clever is not merely imperfect but inverted at the decisive point. The preaching of a crucified Messiah was foolishness to Greeks and a stumblingblock to Jews, and God did not adjust the message to remove the offence. A church that trims the cross to sound credible to the academy has attempted precisely what the chapter forbids, and has usually ended up with neither credibility nor a gospel.
roots_summary: Several Hebrew words for folly stand behind the English — nabal, the moral fool; kesil, the dull and self-confident; 'evil, the obstinate — and the Greek moros, from which English gets its harsher terms.
roots_lines: Hebrew nabal (H5036) — a moral fool, senseless and godless; O foolish people and unwise (Deuteronomy 32:6), and the name of Abigail’s husband.
Hebrew kesil (H3684) — the dull, self-confident fool of Proverbs, who hates knowledge and trusts his own heart.
Hebrew 'evil (H191) — the obstinate fool who despises instruction and will not be corrected.
Hebrew halal (H1984) in its later sense — to be boastful or mad; behind the foolish shall not stand in thy sight (Psalm 5:5).
Greek moros (G3474) — foolish, dull; the wise and foolish virgins (Matthew 25:2) and the foolish things of the world (1 Corinthians 1:27).
usage: O foolish people and unwise (Deuteronomy 32:6) — folly defined as ingratitude to a Redeemer.
Five of them were wise, and five were foolish (Matthew 25:2) — the division is preparedness for a delayed return.
God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise (1 Corinthians 1:27) — the world’s scale of wisdom inverted at the cross.

etymology: From wicked, Middle English wikked, related to wicca, a sorcerer. Webster 1828: in a manner or with motives contrary to the divine law; viciously; corruptly. In the Authorized Version the adverb is the standing word of national confession — we have done wickedly — and of the historians’ verdict on particular kings.
biblical_def: Wickedly is what the penitent says about himself and what the historian says about a king. Nehemiah’s great prayer of confession states both halves of the covenant lawsuit: thou art just in all that is brought upon us; for thou hast done right, but we have done wickedly (Nehemiah 9:33). Daniel confesses in the same terms: We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by departing from thy precepts (Daniel 9:5), and the psalmist joins himself to his fathers in it: We have sinned with our fathers, we have committed iniquity, we have done wickedly (Psalm 106:6). Notice that all three are corporate. The word also carries the verdicts. Manasseh hath done wickedly above all that the Amorites did (2 Kings 21:11). Ahaziah’s mother was his counsellor to do wickedly (2 Chronicles 22:3), which is one of the saddest lines in Chronicles. Lot pleads with the men of Sodom, do not so wickedly (Genesis 19:7). And Job asks the question that keeps the word honest: Will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him? (Job 13:7) — a warning that a man may sin in the very act of defending the Almighty.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WICKEDLY as in a manner or with motives and designs contrary to the divine law; viciously; corruptly; immorally. The KJV uses it above all in the great corporate confessions.
webster_full: WICKEDLY, adv. — In a manner or with motives and designs contrary to the divine law; viciously; corruptly; immorally.
WICKED, a. — Evil in principle or practice; deviating from the divine law; addicted to vice; sinful; immoral.
Webster grounds the definition in the divine law rather than in social harm, which is the biblical footing. Wickedness is measured against a revealed standard, not against consequences.
scriptures: Genesis 19:7
And said, I pray you, brethren, do not so wickedly.
2 Kings 21:11
Because Manasseh king of Judah hath done these abominations, and hath done wickedly above all that the Amorites did, which were before him, and hath made Judah also to sin with his idols:
Nehemiah 9:33
Howbeit thou art just in all that is brought upon us; for thou hast done right, but we have done wickedly:
Daniel 9:5
We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by departing from thy precepts and from thy judgments:
Job 13:7
Will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him?
corruption_summary: The adverb is corrupted by the therapeutic reframing of sin — wickedness described as dysfunction, damage, or unmet need — and by the disappearance of corporate confession, which every biblical instance of the word models.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 9:33, Daniel 9:5, and Psalm 106:6 all say we. Not one of the three men praying was chiefly responsible for what he confesses; Daniel in particular is among the most blameless figures in the Old Testament, and he numbers himself with the rebels without qualification or distancing. The modern instinct, in and out of the church, is the reverse: to identify the guilty party as someone else and to describe one’s own share as a product of circumstance. Where sin is renamed as damage and repentance is replaced by explanation, these prayers become unsayable. They are the church’s pattern for corporate confession and they require the plain word.

Job 13:7 guards the other flank. Job’s friends were defending God’s justice, and Job charges them with speaking wickedly for God. It is possible to sin in the act of contending for the truth — by misrepresenting God’s dealings, by accusing a sufferer to protect a theory, by talking deceitfully in a good cause. The Lord’s own verdict at the end of the book vindicates Job on this point: ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath (Job 42:7). Zeal for orthodoxy does not license careless speech about God or cruel speech about the afflicted.
roots_summary: The Hebrew is chiefly rasha', to be wicked or guilty, and its causative to act wickedly; it is the standard covenant-lawsuit term for the party in the wrong before the judge.
roots_lines: Hebrew rasha' (H7561) — to be wicked, to act wickedly; in the covenant lawsuit, to be the guilty party (Nehemiah 9:33; Daniel 9:5; Psalm 106:6).
Hebrew ra'a' (H7489) — to do evil, to act badly; behind done wickedly above all that the Amorites did (2 Kings 21:11).
Hebrew 'avlah (H5766) — injustice, unrighteousness; speak wickedly for God in Job 13:7 is literally to speak unrighteousness for Him.
The confession formula chata'nu, he'evinu, hirsha'nu — we have sinned, committed iniquity, done wickedly — recurs across Daniel 9, Psalm 106, and 1 Kings 8.
Webster derives English wicked from a root connected with sorcery, which preserves the sense of an active, willed evil rather than a lapse.
usage: Thou hast done right, but we have done wickedly (Nehemiah 9:33) — the covenant lawsuit conceded; God justified and the people condemned.
His mother was his counsellor to do wickedly (2 Chronicles 22:3) — wickedness taught inside a household.
Will ye speak wickedly for God? (Job 13:7) — a man may sin in the act of defending the Almighty.

etymology: Older past participle of drink, used adjectivally. Webster 1828: intoxicated; inebriated; also, saturated with liquor. In the Authorized Version it names a literal sin, a figure for staggering judgment, and, in Revelation, the condition of a persecuting power drunk with the blood of the saints.
biblical_def: The first man in Scripture called drunken is the man who came through the flood: he drank of the wine, and was drunken; and he was uncovered within his tent (Genesis 9:21). Scripture reports the sin of its heroes without softening. Eli misjudges Hannah at prayer — Eli thought she had been drunken (1 Samuel 1:13) — a warning to every pastor about reading a grieving woman’s silence. Then the figure. The wicked and the judged reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end (Psalm 107:27). Isaiah sees a Jerusalem drunken, but not with wine (Isaiah 51:21), staggering under the cup of God’s fury, and a Judah drunken, but not with wine under a spirit of deep sleep (Isaiah 29:9). At Pentecost the charge is answered plainly: these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day (Acts 2:15). Paul rebukes a church whose Supper had become a meal where one is hungry, and another is drunken (1 Corinthians 11:21). And John sees the great harlot drunken with the blood of the saints (Revelation 17:6), the last and most terrible use: a power intoxicated by persecution.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DRUNKEN as intoxicated; inebriated; and, figuratively, saturated or overpowered. The KJV keeps both the literal sin and the figure of a man who cannot stand.
webster_full: DRUNKEN, a. — Intoxicated; inebriated with strong liquor.
Given to habitual excessive drinking; as, a drunken man.
Saturated with liquor or moisture; drenched.
The figurative force in Scripture is Webster’s third sense combined with the first: a man saturated by something until he can no longer stand upright, whether the cup is wine or the wrath of God.
scriptures: Genesis 9:21
And he drank of the wine, and was drunken; and he was uncovered within his tent.
1 Samuel 1:13
Now Hannah, she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard: therefore Eli thought she had been drunken.
Psalm 107:27
They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end.
Acts 2:15
For these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day.
Revelation 17:6
And I saw the woman drunken with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus: and when I saw her, I wondered with great admiration.
corruption_summary: Drunkenness is corrupted in two directions: by a culture that treats it as recreation rather than as a sin Scripture excludes men from the kingdom for, and by a false piety that forbids what God permits and so loses the authority to forbid what He prohibits.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture is not silent or ambiguous. Drunkenness stands in the lists that end shall not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:10; Galatians 5:21), and Paul commands, be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18). The contemporary treatment of intoxication as harmless leisure, and of habitual drunkenness as a condition with no moral dimension at all, cannot be squared with those texts. Scripture does speak of the drunkard with pity and warns of the misery in Proverbs 23, and pastoral care is right to reckon with the ruin it causes in body and household — but it names the thing sin, and it calls for repentance and not merely management.

The opposite error is common in reaction. The Bible blesses wine as God’s gift to make glad the heart of man (Psalm 104:15), our Lord made it at Cana, and Paul counselled Timothy to use a little for his stomach. A church that forbids what Scripture permits has stepped outside its authority, and it will find that its warnings against what Scripture forbids carry less weight for having done so. The line is drawn where Scripture draws it: not at the cup, but at the loss of self-command that Genesis 9:21 records of Noah and 1 Corinthians 11:21 records of the Corinthians at the Lord’s table.
roots_summary: The Hebrew shakar means to become drunk or satiated; the Greek methuo is the ordinary word for intoxication, used literally at Pentecost and figuratively of the harlot in Revelation.
roots_lines: Hebrew shakar (H7937) — to be or become drunk, to be satiated; he drank of the wine, and was drunken (Genesis 9:21).
Hebrew shikkor (H7910) — a drunkard, one intoxicated; the figure in Psalm 107:27 and Isaiah 19:14.
Greek methuo (G3184) — to be drunk; these are not drunken (Acts 2:15), another is drunken (1 Corinthians 11:21), the woman drunken with the blood of the saints (Revelation 17:6).
Greek methe (G3178) — drunkenness, listed among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:21).
The KJV distinguishes drunken as participle-adjective from drunkard as a settled character; the second is the term of the vice lists.
usage: He drank of the wine, and was drunken (Genesis 9:21) — the sin of a righteous man reported without softening.
Eli thought she had been drunken (1 Samuel 1:13) — a priest misjudging a woman’s silent prayer.
The woman drunken with the blood of the saints (Revelation 17:6) — persecution as intoxication.

etymology: From lie, Old English leogan, to speak falsely. Webster 1828: one who knowingly utters falsehood. In Scripture the noun is used with unusual force: of every man over against God, of the devil as the father of lies, and of the professor whose life contradicts his claim to know Christ.
biblical_def: Scripture uses liar to settle three questions. First, who is truthful when God and man disagree: let God be true, but every man a liar; as it is written, That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings (Romans 3:4). Where a man’s account and God’s account conflict, the verdict is fixed in advance. Second, the origin of falsehood: our Lord tells the religious leaders of their father the devil, When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it (John 8:44). Lying is not a lapse in the devil’s case but his native speech. Third, and most searchingly, the test of profession: He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him (1 John 2:4), and If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us (1 John 1:10). John will not permit a Christianity of claims. Proverbs adds the ordinary wisdom — a poor man is better than a liar (Proverbs 19:22), and Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar (Proverbs 30:6), which makes adding to Scripture a species of lying.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LIAR as one who knowingly utters falsehood; one who declares to another as a fact what he knows to be not true. The knowledge is essential: a man mistaken is not thereby a liar.
webster_full: LIAR, n. — A person who knowingly utters falsehood; one who declares to another as a fact what he knows to be not true, and with an intention to deceive him.
One who tells lies habitually; a person given to falsehood.

Webster’s insistence on knowledge and intention matters pastorally. Scripture’s hardest uses of the noun — John 8:44, 1 John 2:4 — are not applied to the mistaken but to those whose profession and practice knowingly diverge.
scriptures: Proverbs 30:6
Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar.
John 8:44

Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.
Romans 3:4
God forbid: yea, let God be true, but every man a liar; as it is written, That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and mightest overcome when thou art judged.
1 John 1:10
If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
1 John 2:4
He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him.
corruption_summary: The word is corrupted wherever truth is treated as a matter of perspective, so that no one can be a liar in the strict sense; and it is evaded wherever a profession of faith is allowed to stand against a contradicting life, which 1 John 2:4 refuses.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 3:4 is the verse that decides the question of whose account governs. Paul is arguing that God’s faithfulness is not overthrown by human unbelief, and he settles it with a fixed rule: let God be true, but every man a liar. That sentence is unavailable to any framework in which truth is constructed by communities or measured by a speaker’s standpoint. If truth is perspectival, then no one lies; there are only competing accounts. Scripture treats falsehood as a real relation between what is said and what is, and it treats God’s word as the fixed term against which every human account is measured.

1 John 2:4 is the harder application, and it is aimed at the church rather than the world. He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar — not weak, not immature, not on a journey, but a liar, and the truth is not in him. John is not teaching justification by obedience; the same letter says that if any man sin we have an advocate with the Father. He is teaching that a profession which produces no obedience is a false statement about oneself. Proverbs 30:6 makes the corresponding warning about Scripture itself: to add to God’s words is to be found a liar, which is why the closed canon and the sufficiency of Scripture are not dry doctrines but matters of honesty.
roots_summary: The Hebrew nouns are from roots for deception and vanity; the Greek pseustes is the standing New Testament term, used of the devil, of the false professor, and of every man over against God.
roots_lines: Hebrew kazab (H3576) — to lie, to be found a liar; lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar (Proverbs 30:6).
Hebrew 'akzab (H391) — deceptive, failing; the figure of waters that fail in Jeremiah 15:18.
Greek pseustes (G5583) — a liar; John 8:44, Romans 3:4, 1 John 1:10 and 2:4.
Greek pseudos (G5579) — a lie, falsehood; the devil speaks of his own when he speaks it.
Revelation 21:8 places all liars in the list of those whose part is in the lake of fire, which measures how seriously Scripture takes the noun.
usage: Let God be true, but every man a liar (Romans 3:4) — the fixed verdict when God’s account and man’s conflict.
He is a liar, and the father of it (John 8:44) — falsehood traced to its origin.
He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar (1 John 2:4) — profession tested by obedience.

etymology: From dis- plus obedient, ultimately Latin obedire, to hearken toward. Webster 1828: neglecting or refusing to obey; violating commands or transgressing lawful authority. The Greek behind the New Testament word carries the sense of refusing to be persuaded — disobedience as a settled unwillingness to hear.
biblical_def: In the New Testament disobedient is a diagnosis, not a description of misbehaviour. Paul quotes Isaiah to describe the nation: All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people (Romans 10:21). He lists disobedient to parents among the marks of a reprobate mind (Romans 1:30) and again among the perils of the last days (2 Timothy 3:2), which tells us the fifth commandment is a diagnostic of a society. He describes false professors: They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate (Titus 1:16). And he includes himself and Titus in the past tense: For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived (Titus 3:3), which is the guard against contempt. Peter locates the deepest use. Christ is precious to those who believe, but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner (1 Peter 2:7), and such stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed (1 Peter 2:8). Paul’s own testimony gives the positive: I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision (Acts 26:19).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DISOBEDIENT as neglecting or refusing to obey; omitting to do what is commanded, or doing what is prohibited; refractory; not observant of duty or lawful authority.
webster_full: DISOBEDIENT, a. — Neglecting or refusing to obey; omitting to do what is commanded, or doing what is forbidden; refractory; not observant of duty or lawful authority.
DISOBEDIENCE, n. — Neglect or refusal to obey; violation of a command or prohibition.

The Greek term the New Testament most often uses adds a nuance Webster’s English does not carry: it is formed from the verb to be persuaded, so that disobedience is at root a refusal to be persuaded by the word.
scriptures: Acts 26:19
Whereupon, O king Agrippa, I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision:
Romans 10:21
But to Israel he saith, All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people.
Titus 1:16
They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate.
Titus 3:3
For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.
1 Peter 2:8
And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed.
corruption_summary: The word is corrupted when disobedience is reframed as authenticity or as a healthy questioning of authority, and when Romans 1:30’s inclusion of disobedient to parents among the marks of a reprobate mind is treated as a cultural relic.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul lists disobedient to parents twice, in Romans 1:30 among the consequences of a mind given over, and in 2 Timothy 3:2 among the marks of the last days. He puts it in company with the worst items on both lists. That placement is not an accident of ancient household order; the fifth commandment is the first with promise, and Paul treats the honour of parents as the school in which a soul learns whether it will submit to any authority at all. A culture that has made adolescent defiance into a developmental stage, and a church that has adopted the same assumption, will find these lists unreadable. Scripture regards a child’s refusal to obey as the seed of a man’s refusal to be persuaded by God.

1 Peter 2:8 is the doctrinally weightiest use, and it must be handled with the care Peter uses. Those who stumble at the word, being disobedient, are those whereunto also they were appointed. The Reformed confessions have never read this as God creating unbelief; the appointment is to the stumbling that follows disobedience, and the disobedience is genuinely the man’s own — he stumbles at the word, which he has heard. Titus 3:3 is the pastoral guard: we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient. No believer who understands the doctrine of election can look down from it, since the only thing that distinguished him was mercy.
roots_summary: The main Greek word is apeithes, unpersuadable, from the verb peitho, to persuade — the same root that gives the New Testament its word for faith as persuasion. Disobedience and unbelief are therefore two faces of one refusal.
roots_lines: Greek apeithes (G545) — unpersuadable, disobedient (Acts 26:19; Romans 1:30; 2 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:16; 3:3).
Greek apeitheo (G544) — to refuse to be persuaded, to disbelieve and so disobey (Romans 10:21; 1 Peter 2:8).
Greek peitho (G3982) — to persuade; the shared root, which is why the KJV can render the same family believe not and obey not.
Greek parakoe (G3876) — a hearing amiss, disobedience; by one man's disobedience many were made sinners (Romans 5:19).
Hebrew marah (H4784) — to be rebellious or contentious; behind the Old Testament portrait Paul quotes in Romans 10:21.
usage: I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision (Acts 26:19) — Paul’s summary of his own conversion and commission.
Disobedient to parents (Romans 1:30; 2 Timothy 3:2) — listed twice among the marks of a mind and an age given over.
We ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient (Titus 3:3) — the guard against contempt for the disobedient.

etymology: From Latin error, a wandering, from errare, to stray. Webster 1828: a wandering from the truth; a mistake in judgment; also, a deviation from law or right. The Latin picture is exact for the biblical use: error is not chiefly a wrong idea but a wrong road, and the New Testament speaks of the error of his way.
biblical_def: Scripture treats error as something a man walks in and can be turned out of. James gives the classic statement: he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins (James 5:20) — a wandering, a turning back, a soul saved. Jude names three errors by the men who ran in them: the way of Cain… the error of Balaam for reward… the gainsaying of Core (Jude 11), so that error has a genealogy and can be identified by its ancestors. Peter warns believers to beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness (2 Peter 3:17), and John draws the sharpest line in the New Testament between two spirits: Hereby know we the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error (1 John 4:6). The Old Testament shows the seriousness. Uzzah reached out to steady the ark and God smote him there for his error; and there he died by the ark of God (2 Samuel 6:7). Ecclesiastes forbids the excuse: neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error (Ecclesiastes 5:6). Sincerity is not a defence in the presence of God; it is the reason a Mediator is necessary.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ERROR as a wandering or deviation from the truth; a mistake in judgment by which men assent to what is not true; and also a deviation from law, right, or duty — a sin or transgression.
webster_full: ERROR, n. [L. error, from erro, to wander.] — A wandering or deviation from the truth; a mistake in judgment, by which men assent to or believe what is not true.
A mistake made in writing or other performance; an inaccuracy.
A wandering from the path of duty or rectitude; a deviation from law or right; sin; transgression.
Webster’s third sense is the biblical one and it is the one modern English has nearly lost. In Scripture an error is not merely something a man thinks; it is something he does, and repents of.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 6:7
And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah; and God smote him there for his error; and there he died by the ark of God.
Ecclesiastes 5:6
Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error: wherefore should God be angry at thy voice, and destroy the work of thine hands?
James 5:20
Let him know, that he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins.
2 Peter 3:17
Ye therefore, beloved, seeing ye know these things before, beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness.
1 John 4:6
We are of God: he that knoweth God heareth us; he that is not of God heareth not us. Hereby know we the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error.
corruption_summary: Error is corrupted when doctrinal wandering is reclassified as diversity of perspective, so that 1 John 4:6’s two spirits become two traditions, and when sincerity is accepted as a defence that Ecclesiastes 5:6 explicitly refuses.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 John 4:6 recognizes exactly two spirits, the spirit of truth and the spirit of error, and it gives a test: whether a man hears the apostolic word. That binary is intolerable to the assumption that every position is a partial view of a whole no one possesses. But the apostle is not describing temperaments; he has just required that every spirit be tried by its confession of Christ come in the flesh. Error in the New Testament is a definable thing with named practitioners — Hymenaeus and Philetus, whose word ate as a canker, Balaam, Core — and the church’s duty is to identify it and turn men from it, which is the ministry James 5:20 describes as saving a soul from death.

Uzzah and Ecclesiastes 5:6 together destroy the modern defence of sincerity. Uzzah’s intention was to protect the ark; his error was that he touched what God had said must be carried by Levites on staves, and the record does not soften the outcome. Ecclesiastes then forbids the plea outright: do not say before the angel that it was an error. This is not a portrait of a God looking for occasions to strike, but of a God whose holiness is real and whose commands about His own worship are not advisory. The remedy Scripture provides is not a lower standard but a Mediator, and it is the same book that tells us the sacrifice for sins of ignorance was appointed before Uzzah was born.
roots_summary: The Hebrew words are from roots meaning to go astray or to err inadvertently; the Greek plane means a wandering, and it gives English planet, the wandering star.
roots_lines: Hebrew shal or shegagah (H7684) — inadvertence, error; the category of sin committed unwittingly (2 Samuel 6:7; Ecclesiastes 5:6).
Hebrew ta'ah (H8582) — to wander, to go astray; the picture behind straying from the way.
Greek plane (G4106) — a wandering, a straying; the error of his way (James 5:20), the error of Balaam (Jude 11), the spirit of error (1 John 4:6).
Greek planetes — a wanderer; Jude 13 calls false teachers wandering stars, from the same root.
Greek agnoema (G51) — a sin of ignorance; the high priest offered for the errors of the people (Hebrews 9:7).
usage: God smote him there for his error (2 Samuel 6:7) — good intention is not a defence where God has commanded a manner.
The error of his way (James 5:20) — error is a road walked, and a man can be turned from it.
The spirit of truth, and the spirit of error (1 John 4:6) — two spirits, not a spectrum, and a test to tell them apart.

etymology: From Old French avengier, from Latin vindicare, to claim or lay legal claim to. Webster 1828: to vindicate; to take satisfaction for an injury by punishing the injurious person. In the Authorized Version the verb is almost always God’s, or the magistrate’s under God, and it is expressly forbidden to the private man.
biblical_def: The law forbids private vengeance in the same verse that commands neighbour-love: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD (Leviticus 19:18). David keeps it under maximum provocation: the LORD judge between me and thee, and the LORD avenge me of thee: but mine hand shall not be upon thee (1 Samuel 24:12) — he asks God for the vengeance and refuses to take it. God claims the act as His own: he will avenge the blood of his servants, and will render vengeance to his adversaries (Deuteronomy 32:43), and He executes it through appointed instruments — thou shalt smite the house of Ahab thy master, that I may avenge the blood of my servants the prophets (2 Kings 9:7). The New Testament repeats the prohibition and grounds it in the claim: Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord (Romans 12:19). Our Lord’s parable of the importunate widow makes crying for vengeance a form of persevering prayer (Luke 18:3-5), and the souls under the altar cry How long, O Lord… dost thou not judge and avenge our blood (Revelation 6:10). Believers are forbidden to take vengeance; they are not forbidden to ask for it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines AVENGE as to vindicate; to take satisfaction for an injury by punishing the injurious person; and notes that in Scripture the act belongs chiefly to God, who declares vengeance to be His own.
webster_full: AVENGE, v.t. — To vindicate; to take satisfaction for an injury by punishing the injurious person; to revenge.
To take satisfaction for, by pain or punishment inflicted on the injuring party; as, to avenge blood.
AVENGER, n. — One who avenges or vindicates; a vindicator.

Webster’s vindicate is the better English word for the biblical idea. The point is not the discharge of anger but the setting right of a wrong, which is why the act belongs to a judge and not to the injured party.
scriptures: Leviticus 19:18
Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.
1 Samuel 24:12
The LORD judge between me and thee, and the LORD avenge me of thee: but mine hand shall not be upon thee.
2 Kings 9:7
And thou shalt smite the house of Ahab thy master, that I may avenge the blood of my servants the prophets, and the blood of all the servants of the LORD, at the hand of Jezebel.
Romans 12:19
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
Revelation 6:10
And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?
corruption_summary: The word is corrupted in two opposite ways: by the revenge culture that makes retaliation a virtue, and by the sentimental reading that treats God’s vengeance as beneath Him — which would leave the martyrs of Revelation 6:10 without an answer.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 12:19 does not tell the believer that his injury does not matter. It tells him that the settling of it belongs to Someone else, and it quotes Deuteronomy 32 to prove it. The prohibition is therefore a comfort as well as a command: a Christian may hand over a wrong precisely because it will be dealt with, not because it will be forgotten. Where that confidence is lost, forgiveness curdles into denial or hardens into grievance. The next verse is remarkable for what it commands instead — if thine enemy hunger, feed him — which is possible only for a man who believes the account has been transferred and not cancelled.

The sentimental error runs the other way and cannot be squared with Revelation 6:10. The souls under the altar are martyrs, they are in heaven, and they cry out to a holy and true Lord asking how long until He avenges their blood. Their prayer is answered, not rebuked. A god who would never avenge would be a god indifferent to the murder of his own, and the moral universe would have no floor. Scripture holds both truths without strain: vengeance belongs to God, He will execute it, the civil magistrate bears the sword as His minister for the present (Romans 13:4), and the private believer keeps his hand off — as David did in the cave, with the man who was hunting him asleep within reach.
roots_summary: The Hebrew root is naqam, to avenge or take vengeance; the Greek ekdikeo means to vindicate or execute justice out of a legal claim, and its noun is the New Testament word for vengeance.
roots_lines: Hebrew naqam (H5358) — to avenge, to take vengeance; forbidden to the private man in Leviticus 19:18, claimed by God in Deuteronomy 32:43.
Hebrew go'el ha-dam — the avenger of blood, the appointed kinsman whose office the cities of refuge regulate (Numbers 35).
Greek ekdikeo (G1556) — to vindicate, to avenge; the importunate widow’s plea (Luke 18:3) and the martyrs’ cry (Revelation 6:10).
Greek ekdikesis (G1557) — vengeance; Vengeance is mine; I will repay (Romans 12:19).
Greek ekdikos (G1558) — an avenger; the magistrate is God’s revenger to execute wrath (Romans 13:4).
usage: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge (Leviticus 19:18) — the prohibition stands in the same verse as the command to love the neighbour.
The LORD avenge me of thee: but mine hand shall not be upon thee (1 Samuel 24:12) — David asks for it and refuses to take it.
Avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath (Romans 12:19) — the account is transferred, not cancelled.

etymology: From Old French jalous, from Late Latin zelosus, full of zeal, from Greek zelos. Webster 1828: suspicious that we do not enjoy the affection or respect of others; and, of God, solicitous for His own honour. The word is the same root as zeal, which is why Scripture can predicate it of God without any taint of pettiness.
biblical_def: God calls jealousy His name. Thou shalt worship no other god: for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God (Exodus 34:14). It is not an occasional mood but an attribute bound to His exclusive right to be worshipped, which is why it appears in the second commandment and in Moses’ warnings: the LORD thy God is a consuming fire, even a jealous God (Deuteronomy 4:24); the LORD thy God is a jealous God among you (Deuteronomy 6:15). Joshua presses it on a people making an easy profession: he is an holy God; he is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions nor your sins (Joshua 24:19). The jealousy is also for His people’s good: Then will the LORD be jealous for his land, and pity his people (Joel 2:18), and He acts jealous for my holy name (Ezekiel 39:25). The marriage figure explains it. A husband’s jealousy over his wife is a covenant emotion, and Numbers 5 makes it a legal category. Paul takes the figure up without apology: I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). Jealousy of that kind is the opposite of indifference.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines JEALOUS as suspicious of rivalry in love or honour; and, in the divine sense, solicitous to maintain one’s own honour and the purity of worship. He notes explicitly that God is jealous of His own glory and worship.
webster_full: JEALOUS, a. — Suspicious; apprehensive of rivalship; uneasy through fear that another has withdrawn or may withdraw from one the affections of a person he loves.
Emulous; full of competition; zealous.
Solicitous to maintain or defend; as, jealous of one’s honour or reputation.
Applied to God, it denotes His solicitude for His own glory and the purity of His worship — the LORD, whose name is Jealous.

Webster’s progression is the theological answer to the modern objection. Human jealousy is corrupted by insecurity; divine jealousy is the zeal of a Husband with an absolute right, which no rival can either threaten or deserve.
scriptures: Exodus 34:14
For thou shalt worship no other god: for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God:
Deuteronomy 4:24
For the LORD thy God is a consuming fire, even a jealous God.
Joshua 24:19
And Joshua said unto the people, Ye cannot serve the LORD: for he is an holy God; he is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions nor your sins.
Joel 2:18
Then will the LORD be jealous for his land, and pity his people.
2 Corinthians 11:2
For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
corruption_summary: Divine jealousy is corrupted when it is read through human insecurity — as though God were petty or possessive — and it is quietly deleted whenever the second commandment is treated as a comment on ancient idols rather than as a live claim on worship.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard objection says that jealousy is a vice, and a jealous God is therefore an unworthy one. It rests on a confusion. Human jealousy is usually sinful because it is either envy of what another rightly has, or a suspicion born of insecurity about a claim we do not actually possess. Neither applies to God. He has an absolute right to the worship of His creatures, and no rival has any claim on it at all. The husband analogy Paul uses in 2 Corinthians 11:2 makes the point: a husband indifferent to his wife’s adultery is not admirably tolerant, he is a man who does not love her. Divine jealousy is the necessary form love takes when the covenant is exclusive and it is being violated.

The quieter corruption is practical. Exodus 34:14 states the jealousy as the ground of a prohibition on other gods, and the second commandment attaches it to images. Where worship is arranged according to what moves an audience rather than what God has commanded, the jealousy has not been argued away but simply ignored. Joshua 24:19 is the sobering case: a congregation making an enthusiastic profession is told Ye cannot serve the LORD, because the God they were volunteering to serve is holy and jealous. Joshua was not discouraging them from covenant; he was insisting they count the cost of one. And the same jealousy is their hope, since a God jealous for His holy name will not let His people go.
roots_summary: The Hebrew qanna' is used only of God and describes His zeal for His exclusive covenant right; the related noun covers both the husband’s jealousy of Numbers 5 and God’s. The Greek zelos gives English both zeal and jealousy.
roots_lines: Hebrew qanna' (H7067) — jealous; used in Scripture only of God (Exodus 34:14; Deuteronomy 4:24; 6:15; Joshua 24:19).
Hebrew qin'ah (H7068) — jealousy, zeal, ardour; the spirit of jealousy in the law of Numbers 5 and the LORD’s zeal for His land in Joel 2:18.
Hebrew El Qanna' — a jealous God, a divine title attached to the second commandment (Exodus 20:5).
Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal or jealousy according to context; I am jealous over you with godly jealousy (2 Corinthians 11:2).
The single Greek root behind English zeal and jealousy explains why Scripture can predicate the affection of God without predicating the vice.
usage: The LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God (Exodus 34:14) — jealousy stated as a name, not a mood.
He is an holy God; he is a jealous God (Joshua 24:19) — spoken to a congregation making a cheap profession.
I am jealous over you with godly jealousy (2 Corinthians 11:2) — the pastor’s duty to guard a betrothed church.
